blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 4 (Work, Energy and Power), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question of 5 marks (define, explain, derive) is followed by a numerical of 3 marks on the same topic. Each question has a model answer; the numericals are solved step by step.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define work done by a constant force. Derive its formula when the force makes an angle θ with the displacement, and show how the work is represented on a force-displacement graph. State when the work is positive, zero and negative. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: When a constant force F displaces an object through a displacement d in the direction of the force, work W is the product of the magnitude of the force and the magnitude of the displacement:
W = Fd ... (4.1)
If the displacement is zero, no work is done even if a large force is applied (e.g. pushing a wall).

Force at an angle: The force may not always be in the direction of the displacement (Fig. 4.2). If F makes an angle θ with d, only the component of force along the displacement, F cos θ (Fig. 4.3), does work. The work is the product of this component and the magnitude of the displacement:
W = (F cos θ)d = Fd cos θ ... (4.2)
or W = F⃗·d⃗ ... (4.3)
Eq. (4.3) shows that work is a scalar quantity. Its SI unit is the joule: 1 J = 1 N m.

Graph: Plot displacement along the x-axis and force along the y-axis (Fig. 4.4). A constant force gives a horizontal straight line. If F and d are in the same direction, the work is Fd, which is the shaded area of rectangle OPQR. Hence the area under a force-displacement curve represents the work done. If F is not along d, the graph is plotted between F cos θ and d.

Sign of work:
θ < 90°: positive work
θ = 90°: no work is done
θ > 90°: negative work

book_ref.quote: Let us consider an object which is being pulled by a constant force F.

blocks.prompt: 2 A gardener pushes a lawn mower 15 m along level ground with a force of 120 N directed along the handle at 30° to the ground. A frictional force of 80 N opposes the motion. Find (i) the work done by the gardener's force (ii) the work done by friction (iii) the net work done on the mower. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use W = Fd cos θ for each force: θ = 30° for the push and θ = 180° for friction; then add.

book_ref.quote: the work done is equal to the product of the component of force along the direction of the displacement

blocks.prompt: 3 What is a variable force? Show that the work done by a variable force in moving a particle between two points equals the area under the F cos θ versus d curve. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Variable force: a force that does not remain constant during the process of doing work, e.g. gravity on a rocket moving away from the Earth (varies as the inverse square of the distance from the Earth's centre) and the force of a spring (increases with stretch).

Derivation: Let a particle move along a path in the xy plane from P to Q (Fig. 4.5). Divide the path into n short intervals of displacement Δd₁, Δd₂, …, Δdₙ, with forces F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ acting during them. In each small interval the force is approximately constant, so
ΔW₁ = F⃗₁·Δd⃗₁ = F₁ cos θ₁ Δd₁
ΔW₂ = F⃗₂·Δd⃗₂ = F₂ cos θ₂ Δd₂, and so on.
The total work is the sum:
W_total = ΔW₁ + ΔW₂ + … + ΔWₙ = F₁ cos θ₁ Δd₁ + F₂ cos θ₂ Δd₂ + … + Fₙ cos θₙ Δdₙ
W_total = Σ Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ (i = 1 to n) ... (4.4)

Graphical meaning: Plot F cos θ against d (Fig. 4.6). The iᵗʰ shaded rectangle has area Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ, the work done in the iᵗʰ interval, so Eq. 4.4 is the sum of the areas of all the rectangles. With more and smaller intervals the result becomes more accurate; letting each Δd approach zero gives the exact result:
W_total = lim (Δd → 0) Σ Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ ... (4.5)
In this limit, the total area of the rectangles approaches the area between the F cos θ versus d curve and the x-axis from P to Q (Fig. 4.7).

Hence the work done by a variable force between two points is equal to the area under the F cos θ versus d curve between them.

book_ref.quote: The path has been divided into n short intervals of displacements

blocks.prompt: 4 A force acting on a body along its motion increases uniformly from 0 to 12 N as the body moves from d = 0 to d = 3 m, stays at 12 N from d = 3 m to d = 7 m, and then decreases uniformly to zero at d = 9 m. Find the total work done by the force. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Work = area under the force-distance graph: a triangle, a rectangle and a triangle.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the work done by the force as the object moves from d = 0 to d = 6 m.

steps: From 0 to 3 m (triangle): ½ × 3 m × 12 N = 18 J
From 3 m to 7 m (rectangle): 4 m × 12 N = 48 J
From 7 m to 9 m (triangle): ½ × 2 m × 12 N = 12 J

blocks.prompt: 5 Define conservative and non-conservative forces. Show that the gravitational force is a conservative force by finding the work done by it along three different paths. Give examples of both kinds of force. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Conservative force: If the work done by a force in moving an object between two points is independent of the path followed, or the work done in a closed path is zero, the force is a conservative force.
Non-conservative force: A force is non-conservative if the work done by it between two points or in a closed path depends on the path of motion.

Gravity is conservative: An object of mass m is displaced with constant speed from A to B (B is a height h above A) along three paths (Fig. 4.9). The gravitational force is its weight mg.
Path 1 (ADB): Along AD the weight is perpendicular to the path, so work = 0. Along DB, mg is opposite to the displacement (θ = 180°), so work = −mgh.
W_ADB = 0 + (−mgh) = −mgh
Path 2 (ACB): Along AC the work is −mgh; along CB it is zero.
W_ACB = −mgh + 0 = −mgh
Path 3 (curved): Break the curve into a series of horizontal and vertical steps (Fig. 4.10). No work is done along the horizontal steps because mg is perpendicular to them; work is done only along the vertical steps:
W_AB = −mg(Δy₁ + Δy₂ + Δy₃ + … + Δyₙ)
As Δy₁ + Δy₂ + … + Δyₙ = h, W_AB = −mgh
The work is −mgh along every path, so work done by the gravitational force is independent of the path followed; along a closed path such as ACBA it is −mgh + mgh = 0. Hence gravity is a conservative force.

Non-conservative example: Kinetic friction acts opposite to the motion and does negative work equal to friction × length of path, so more work is done over a longer path; its total work in a closed path is not zero.

Examples:
Conservative: gravitational force, electrostatic force, elastic spring force.
Non-conservative: kinetic friction, air resistance, tension in a string, normal force, propulsion force of a rocket.

book_ref.quote: Consider an object of mass m being displaced with constant speed from point A to B along various paths

blocks.prompt: 6 A 4 kg box is raised from the floor to a platform 2.5 m high, once by lifting it straight up and once by pushing it up a 6.0 m long ramp on which the kinetic friction is 10 N. Find (i) the work done by gravity along each path (ii) the work done by friction along the ramp (iii) the total work done by gravity and by friction if the box is pushed up the ramp and slid back down it to the floor. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Gravity's work depends only on the change in height (−mgh); friction's work is −f × path length and keeps adding up.

book_ref.quote: When an object slides over a surface, the kinetic frictional force acts opposite to the motion

steps: (i) W_gravity = −mgh = −4 × 9.8 × 2.5 = −98 J along both paths (independent of path)
(iii) Up and back down (closed path): gravity −98 J + 98 J = 0
Friction acts opposite to the motion both ways: −60 J + (−60 J) = −120 J, not zero
blocks.final_answer: (i) −98 J on both paths (ii) −60 J (iii) gravity 0, friction −120 J: gravity is conservative, friction is non-conservative

blocks.prompt: 7 Define power, average power and instantaneous power. Show that power is the dot product of force and velocity. Define the watt and the kilowatt-hour, and express 1 kW h in joules. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Need: The definition of work does not show whether the work is done in one second or in one hour; the rate of doing work is of interest in practical applications.

Power: Power is the measure of the rate at which work is being done.
Average power: If work ΔW is done in time interval Δt,
P_av = ΔW/Δt ... (4.6)
Instantaneous power: If work is a function of time, the power at any instant is
P = lim (Δt → 0) ΔW/Δt ... (4.7)
where ΔW is the work done in the short interval Δt.

Power = force · velocity:
Since ΔW = F⃗·Δd⃗,
P = F⃗·Δd⃗/Δt = F⃗·(Δd⃗/Δt)
Since Δd⃗/Δt = v⃗,
P = F⃗·v⃗ ... (4.8)

Watt: The SI unit of power is the watt, one joule of work done in one second (1 W = 1 J s⁻¹). In electrical measurements work is sometimes expressed in watt second.

Kilowatt-hour: The commercial unit of electrical energy. One kilowatt-hour is the work done in one hour by an agency whose power is one kilowatt.
1 kW h = 1000 W × 3600 s = 3.6 × 10⁶ J = 3.6 MJ

book_ref.quote: The rate, at which work is done, is often of interest in practical applications.

blocks.prompt: 8 A lift of total mass 800 kg is raised at a steady speed through a height of 20 m in 16 s. Find (i) the work done against gravity (ii) the power of the motor from P = W/t (iii) the same power from P = Fv. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: At steady speed the lifting force equals the weight mg; work = mgh, and both P = W/t and P = Fv must give the same power.

book_ref.quote: A 70 kg man runs up a long flight of stairs in 4.0 s.

blocks.prompt: 9 Define kinetic energy. Derive the expression K.E. = ½mv² for a body of mass m moving with speed v. What is its unit? (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: Kinetic energy is the energy possessed by a body due to its motion; it is the ability of a body to do work due to its motion.

Derivation: Consider a car of mass m moving with speed v. If its engine is switched off, it still covers some distance d before stopping. While moving, it does work against the force of friction f of the road, i.e. it exerts a force equal in magnitude to f. The work done by the car due to its motion is fd, so
kinetic energy of the car = fd
By Newton's second law, F = ma. As the car slows down, its acceleration is negative because it is produced by friction acting opposite to the motion:
f = −ma, or a = −f/m
Third equation of motion: 2aS = vf² − vi²
Here vi = v, vf = 0, S = d, a = −f/m
2 × (−f/m) d = 0 − v²
fd = ½mv²
Since fd is the kinetic energy of the body,
Kinetic energy = ½mv² ... (4.9)

Unit: Kinetic energy equals the work the body is capable of doing, so its unit is that of work, the joule (J).

book_ref.quote: Consider a car running with a constant speed on a road.

blocks.prompt: 10 A car of weight 14700 N is moving at 20 m s⁻¹. Its brakes bring it to rest in 50 m. Find (i) its mass (ii) its kinetic energy (iii) the average force of friction on it. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Get m from w = mg; the K.E. ½mv² equals the work fd done before stopping.

book_ref.quote: The kinetic energy of the car is equal to the work done by it before stopping

blocks.prompt: 11 Define absolute gravitational potential energy. Derive the expression U = −GMm/r for a body at a distance r from the centre of the Earth, and write its value at the Earth's surface. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Definition: The absolute gravitational potential energy of an object at a position is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing it from that position to infinity, where the force of gravity becomes zero.

Why mgh fails: mgh is true only near the Earth's surface where gravity is nearly constant. If a body is moved a large distance, from point 1 to N (Fig. 4.11), the force varies inversely as the square of the distance.

Derivation: Divide the distance from 1 to N into small steps of length Δr so that the force is constant in each step. Let r₁ and r₂ be the distances of points 1 and 2 from the Earth's centre O. The centre of the first step is at
r = (r₁ + r₂)/2; as r₂ = r₁ + Δr, r = r₁ + Δr/2 ... (4.10)
Force at the centre of this step: F = GMm/r² ... (4.11)
Squaring (4.10): r² = r₁² + 2r₁(Δr/2) + (Δr/2)²
As (Δr)² << r₁², it is neglected: r² = r₁² + r₁Δr
Putting Δr = r₂ − r₁: r² = r₁² + r₁(r₂ − r₁) = r₁r₂
So F = GMm/(r₁r₂) ... (4.12)
Work from 1 to 2 (displacement opposite to gravity, θ = 180°):
W₁→₂ = F Δr cos 180° = −GMm Δr/(r₁r₂) = −GMm (r₂ − r₁)/(r₁r₂)
W₁→₂ = −GMm (1/r₁ − 1/r₂)
Similarly W₂→₃ = −GMm (1/r₂ − 1/r₃), …, W(N−1)→N = −GMm (1/r(N−1) − 1/r_N)
Adding all steps, the middle terms cancel:
W_total = −GMm (1/r₁ − 1/r_N)
If N is at infinity, r_N = ∞ and 1/r_N = 0:
W_total = −GMm/r₁
By definition this is the absolute P.E., so at a distance r:
U = −GMm/r

At the Earth's surface (r = R): U_g = −GMm/R ... (4.13)
The negative sign shows that the Earth's gravitational field for mass m is attractive. As r increases, U becomes less negative, i.e. P.E. increases; to take the body from the surface to infinity, work GMm/R must be done on it.

book_ref.quote: In order to overcome this difficulty, we divide the distance between points 1 and N into small steps

blocks.prompt: 12 A 500 kg satellite is taken from the Earth's surface to a distance 2R from the Earth's centre. Taking GM = 4.0 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻² and R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m, find (i) its absolute P.E. at the surface (ii) its absolute P.E. at 2R (iii) the work needed to raise it from R to 2R. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use U = −GMm/r at r = R and r = 2R; the work needed is the increase in U.

book_ref.quote: Now the absolute potential energy on the surface of the Earth is found by putting r = R

blocks.prompt: 13 Define escape velocity. Derive the expressions v_esc = √(2GM/R) and v_esc = √(2gR), and state its approximate value for the Earth. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Idea: An object projected upward comes back because gravity acts downward. With a larger initial velocity it rises higher; at a certain initial velocity it does not return and escapes out of the influence of gravity.

Definition: The initial velocity with which an object goes out of the Earth's gravitational field is the escape velocity.

Derivation: The escape velocity gives the initial kinetic energy that carries the body to an infinite distance from the Earth's surface:
Initial K.E. = ½mv_esc²
The work done in lifting the body from the surface to infinity equals the increase in P.E.:
Increase in P.E. = 0 − (−GMm/R) = GMm/R
where M and R are the mass and radius of the Earth. The body escapes if the initial K.E. equals this increase in P.E.:
½mv_esc² = GMm/R
v_esc = √(2GM/R) ... (4.14)
As g = GM/R², GM/R = gR, so
v_esc = √(2gR) ... (4.15)

The mass m of the body cancels, so the escape velocity does not depend on the mass of the body. For the Earth, v_esc is approximately 11 km s⁻¹ (11.2 km s⁻¹ in the table of escape speeds).

book_ref.quote: The escape velocity corresponds to the initial kinetic energy gained by the body, which carries it to an infinite distance from the surface of the Earth.

blocks.prompt: 14 The acceleration due to gravity at the surface of the Moon is 1.6 m s⁻² and its radius is 1.74 × 10⁶ m. Find the escape velocity from the Moon and compare it with the value in the chapter's table. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Put the Moon's g and R into v_esc = √(2gR).

book_ref.quote: The value of v_esc comes out to be approximately 11 km s⁻¹.

steps: ≈ 2.4 km s⁻¹, the same as the Moon's value in the table of escape speeds

blocks.prompt: 15 State and derive the work-energy theorem. Explain why it holds for any direction of the force and for a varying force. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Statement: The change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by a net force. It is also called the work-energy principle.

Derivation: Whenever work is done on a body, its energy increases. Let a force F act on a body of mass m, initially moving with velocity vi, through a distance d, increasing its velocity to vf. From the third equation of motion:
2ad = vf² − vi²
a = (1/2d)(vf² − vi²) ... (4.16)
From Newton's second law, F = ma, or
a = F/m ... (4.17)
Comparing (4.16) and (4.17):
F/m = (1/2d)(vf² − vi²)
Fd = ½mvf² − ½mvi² ... (4.18)
W = change in K.E. = (K.E.)f − (K.E.)i = ½mvf² − ½mvi²

Generality: The theorem applies for any direction of the force relative to the displacement. If an object with kinetic energy pushes or pulls another object, the work is taken as negative and its kinetic energy decreases. The theorem remains valid even if the force varies from point to point.

book_ref.quote: This expression is the work-energy theorem. It states that:

blocks.prompt: 16 A 40 kg block starts down a 30° slope at 2.0 m s⁻¹. The kinetic frictional force on it is 80 N. Using the work-energy theorem, find its speed after it has slid 20 m down the slope (sin 30° = 0.5). (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find the net force along the slope (mg sin θ − f), its work Fd, and add it to the initial K.E.

book_ref.quote: A motorcycle rider weighing 60 kg is coasting down a 24° slope.

steps: W = ½mvf² − ½mvi²: 2320 = ½ × 40 × vf² − ½ × 40 × (2.0)²

blocks.prompt: 17 Show that for a freely falling body (air friction ignored) the total energy at every point of its fall is mgh, and hence that loss in P.E. equals gain in K.E. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Consider a body of mass m at rest at height h (Fig. 4.12).

At A (top): P.E. = mgh, K.E. = 0, total = mgh.

At B (fallen a distance x):
P.E. = mg(h − x)
K.E. = ½mvB²
From vf² = vi² + 2gS with vf = vB, vi = 0, S = x: vB² = 2gx
K.E. = ½m(2gx) = mgx
Total energy = mg(h − x) + mgx = mgh ... (4.19)

At C (just before striking the ground): P.E. = 0
vC² = vi² + 2gh = 2gh (vi = 0)
K.E. = ½mvC² = ½m × 2gh = mgh
So at C the K.E. equals the original P.E.

Conclusion: As the body falls its velocity, and so its K.E., increases, while its height, and so its P.E., decreases; the total stays mgh. Between heights h₁ and h₂ with velocities v₁ and v₂ (Fig. 4.13):
Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E.
mg(h₁ − h₂) = ½m(v₂² − v₁²) ... (4.20)
This is true only when frictional force is not considered.

book_ref.quote: Consider a body of mass m at rest, at a height h above the surface of the Earth

blocks.prompt: 18 A 2 kg ball is released from rest at a height of 30 m. Ignoring air friction, find its P.E., K.E. and total energy (i) at the start (ii) after it has fallen 10 m (iii) after it has fallen 20 m, and (iv) its speed just before it hits the ground. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: P.E. = mg(h − x), K.E. = mgx; the total stays mgh. At the ground all of it is K.E.

book_ref.quote: Let us calculate P.E. and K.E. at the position B when the body has fallen a distance x, ignoring air friction.

blocks.final_answer: Total energy stays 588 J; speed at the ground = 24.2 m s⁻¹

blocks.prompt: 19 Explain how the conservation of energy of a falling body is modified when a frictional force acts on it. Derive mgh = ½mv² + fh and write the corresponding relation for a body moving up against friction. (5 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Without friction, all the P.E. lost by a falling body becomes K.E.: mg(h₁ − h₂) = ½m(v₂² − v₁²). This is true only when friction is not considered.

With friction: Let a frictional force f act on the body during its downward motion through height h. Part of the P.E. is used in doing work against friction, equal to fh. Only the remaining P.E., mgh − fh, is converted into K.E.:
mgh − fh = ½mv²
mgh = ½mv² + fh ... (4.21)
Thus:
Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E. + Work done against friction

Conversely, for a body moving up (or a car coasting uphill with its engine off), its K.E. is partly converted into P.E. and partly used in doing work against friction:
Loss of K.E. = Gain in P.E. + Work done against friction
½m(vi² − vf²) = mgh + fd, where d is the distance moved against friction.

On a level road (no change in height), all the K.E. is used against friction before the body stops: ½mv² = fS.

book_ref.quote: If we assume that a frictional force f is present during the downward motion

blocks.prompt: 20 A 1000 kg car moving at 15 m s⁻¹ has its engine stop at point P. It coasts 30 m up a slope to point Q, which is 2.0 m higher than P, against a frictional force of 150 N. Find (i) its speed at Q (ii) how far it goes on a level road beyond Q before stopping, against the same friction. (3 marks)
blocks.explanation: From P to Q: loss of K.E. = gain in P.E. + work against friction. Beyond Q on level road: ½mv² = fS.

book_ref.quote: How far beyond Q will it go before coming to rest?
